Build an argumentative essay: introduction, thesis, arguments for, arguments against, conclusion.
Introduce arguments with B2 formulas: Für … spricht vor allem, dass… / Ein weiteres Argument ist… / Nicht zuletzt…
Present and refute objections: Kritiker wenden ein… / Dem ist entgegenzuhalten… / Dieses Argument greift zu kurz, weil…
End in a balanced way: Abschließend lässt sich festhalten… / Wägt man die Argumente ab, …
Use data and examples as evidence (Studien belegen, dass…).

It's July 2034. Lena and Andrei are taking the night train to Sibiu, to Mara's church wedding. For her evening class Lena has to write an essay: “Ist die Ehe noch zeitgemäß?” (Is marriage still in keeping with the times?) Andrei is helping her.
Right. The thesis: marriage is an outdated institution. How do I start?
Not with the thesis. First an introduction. For example: “Fewer and fewer couples are getting married. It cannot be denied that marriage has lost some of its importance in recent decades.”
Good. And then my arguments against. One: you don't need a stamp from the registry office to love each other.
More elegant: “The main argument against marriage is that love does not need a legal form.” And the second?
Two: almost one in three marriages ends in divorce. That's in a study I read.
“In addition, studies show that about a third of marriages end in divorce.” And now comes the other side.
Do I have to? I'm against marriage, after all.
A good essay weighs things up. “Supporters object that marriage provides legal security, for example in case of illness or with inheritance.” And then you refute it or partly agree with them.
“Against this it can be argued that today this can also be arranged by a contract.” Does that sound good?
“In conclusion, it can be said that marriage is no longer necessary for many people.” Hm. But we're on our way to a wedding right now. The second in three months.
Maybe you need one more argument for. Last but not least: some people simply want to say in front of everyone that they belong to each other. Without any contract.
1. The structure of the argumentative essay
the topic, why it's relevant now
In den letzten Jahren … / Immer mehr Menschen … / Es lässt sich nicht leugnen, dass …
Im Folgenden soll erörtert werden, ob …
Für … spricht vor allem, dass … / Ein weiteres Argument ist …
Kritiker wenden ein, dass … / Dem ist entgegenzuhalten, dass …
Abschließend lässt sich festhalten, dass … / Wägt man die Argumente ab, …
In the Goethe B2 exam (Schreiben Teil 1) you write an opinion text of ~150 words for a forum, covering four required points. This structure helps you not to forget any of them.
2. How to introduce and link arguments
Für … spricht vor allem / in erster Linie, dass …
Darüber hinaus … / Hinzu kommt, dass … / Ein weiterer Aspekt ist …
Nicht zuletzt … / Besonders ins Gewicht fällt, dass …
Studien belegen, dass … / Dies zeigt sich zum Beispiel daran, dass …
Kritiker wenden ein, dass … / Man könnte einwenden, dass … / Befürworter argumentieren, dass …
Dem ist entgegenzuhalten, dass … / Dieses Argument greift zu kurz, weil … / Das trifft nur bedingt zu.
Zwar ist es richtig, dass …, aber … / Dieser Einwand ist berechtigt, dennoch …
“Dem ist entgegenzuhalten” = the “sein + zu” construction from chapter 71: “this must / can be countered”. It's one of the most elegant B2 formulas.
In conclusion, it can be said that…
If you weigh up the arguments, you come to the conclusion that…
In my opinion, the advantages / disadvantages outweigh the others.
Don't bring in new arguments in the conclusion. Sum up and say clearly what you think.
Critics object that it is outdated.
Against this it can be argued that it provides security.
In addition, tradition plays a role.
Studies show that a third of marriages end in divorce.
Last but not least, marriage is also a promise.
Dieses Argument greift zu kurz, weil …
Where do you not bring in new arguments?
It's only true under certain conditions.
If you weigh up the arguments, you come to the conclusion…
In addition, it must be said that…

The Orthodox church in Sibiu's Lower Town was small, old and so full of icons that Lena, at the entrance, didn't know where to look first. The walls were painted from top to bottom, with saints in gold, blue and red, who all looked very serious. It smelled of incense and of the lilies Elena had put in every corner early that morning. Outside it was hot, thirty-eight degrees, the hottest July day in years, and inside more than a hundred people stood crowded next to each other, because in an Orthodox church you don't sit down. Lena hadn't known that. She was wearing new shoes.

She stood next to Andrei in the third row, between an old aunt who kept lighting candles and a little boy who giggled every time the priest sang. Her feet began to hurt after twenty minutes; after forty she could no longer feel them. But she didn't move. It was her third time in Sibiu. The first time in the summer seven years ago, with Mara, when everything was still new; the second time at Christmas three years ago, with Andrei. Back then everything had been new: the language, the city, the family who had welcomed her like a daughter, even though at the time she was only Mara's friend from Berlin. Now she was more. Only nobody knew yet how much more.

The wedding ceremony lasted an hour and a half. Lena understood almost nothing. The priest, a tall man with a long grey beard and a deep, singing voice, sang most of the time, and a small choir in the gallery answered him. Mara and Jakob stood at the front, Jakob in a dark suit that was obviously too warm for him in that heat, Mara in a white dress with embroidery sewn by Elena, after the pattern of the ie (traditional blouse) her own grandmother had worn at her wedding. Then crowns were placed on their heads, golden crowns, and the priest led them three times around a small table while the choir sang.

In front of the church Dan had been waiting for them, in his only suit, the same one he had worn at the court for the apostille. He shook Lena's hand, then hesitated and hugged her after all, briefly and tightly, the way you hug someone who is part of the family. Andrei saw it, smiled and said nothing. During the whole train journey he had hardly spoken, apart from Lena's essay, and Lena had thought he was simply tired.

Andrei stood next to Lena and quietly translated what he could. That the crowns meant the two of them were now king and queen of their own little kingdom. That the dance around the table meant the path they would walk together from now on. That the wine they both had to drink from was life, with its sweet and bitter parts. Lena listened and saw the crowns and the wine and Mara's face, which was radiant with happiness, and thought of her essay. “Marriage is an outdated institution,” she had written. And suddenly the sentence seemed very thin to her. Like an argument that falls short.

Ludwig had stayed in Berlin. He had thought about it a lot. He would have liked to come, but at eighty-six and with a knee that protested at every staircase, twenty-four hours on the night train were, as he put it, “an essay in which the arguments against clearly outweigh the others”. Besides, he didn't want to leave Grete alone; since Friedrich's death she had sat with him at the café every afternoon doing crosswords, faster than he did. But he was there all the same. Andrei had fixed his phone to a column next to the altar, on a video call, and in Berlin, in the café “Bei Ingrid”, Ludwig and Grete sat in front of Lena's laptop and saw everything, the crowns, the wine, the dance, and Grete said: “So much gold. So much singing. Friedrich would have found it dreadful. And then he would have cried.”

The party afterwards was in the garden of the Ionescu family's old house, under the walnut tree, at long tables that Dan and his neighbours had built from planks and trestles. There were sarmale and mici (grilled meat rolls) and ciorbă (sour soup) and cozonac (sweet bread), and wine from the village of Elena's brother, and țuică, of which Jakob drank two glasses before someone explained to him that you don't drink it like water. A band of three old men with violin, accordion and cimbalom played, and the hora began at eight and, by Lena's estimate, never ended. Mrs Lorenz from Thuringia, who had come too, danced with Dan, even though neither of them knew the steps, and they both laughed so much that they kept tripping.

Lena danced too, with Andrei, with Dan, with the little boy who had giggled in church and who turned out to be Andrei's second cousin, and with a row of aunts whose names she immediately forgot. At one point she sat down at the edge, tired, took off her new shoes and went on dancing barefoot, in the warm grass under the walnut tree, and Elena came over to her and said in her slow, careful German: “You dance like one of us.” Lena didn't know what to answer. She simply hugged Elena, and Elena smelled of lilies, incense and sarmale.

At eleven at night, when the hora took a break and the musicians were drinking wine, Andrei took Lena by the hand and led her to the back, to the end of the garden, to the little wooden shed that had been his grandfather's workshop. There, in the dark, lit only by the lanterns in the garden, stood his father's beehives, and behind them, on the wall of the shed, hung a shelf with fifty-two little wooden birds. Andrei had taken them out of his mother's cupboard in the spring and set them out here, all fifty-two, in a row. The last one, with the crooked eyes, stood right at the end.
Above the garden were the stars, more of them than Lena had ever seen in Berlin.

“Why did you bring them here?” Lena asked quietly. Andrei didn't answer at once. He ran his finger over the first bird, which his grandfather had carved in 1977, a little robin, roughly worked, then over the tenth, the twentieth, the fortieth, which became finer and finer, more and more alive, as if the old man had worked all his life on the same bird and understood it a little better every year. “My grandfather used to say,” Andrei said at last, “that you never understand a person completely. Every year you carve a new bird and you get a little closer to them. That's what marriage is, he said. When I was a child I didn't understand.”

No. Not quite at the end. Lena saw it when her eyes had got used to the dark. Next to the fifty-second bird stood a fifty-third. It was smaller than the others, freshly carved, the wood still pale, and it was holding something in its beak. Something small and shiny. Lena went closer. It was a ring. A thin silver ring with a little gold bee on it. A bee like the one on the silver ring Andrei had given her five years ago at Christmas, which she had worn every day since. Only this bee was gold.

Lena, on the train you wrote that marriage is an outdated institution. I helped you. I even gave you the best phrases. But I kept back one last argument. For the other side. It isn't very scientific. There's no study about it. It's just this: I want to say in front of all the people we love that I belong to you. Here, where my grandfather carved birds for my grandmother for fifty-one years. Will you marry me?

Lena said nothing for a long time. From the garden came the sound of the musicians starting to play again, softly, a slow doina (Romanian lament) that drifted over the dark gardens of the Lower Town. The bees in the hives were humming in their sleep. And then Lena laughed and cried, both at once, and said: “Andrei Ionescu, you're impossible. You helped me write an essay against marriage on the train so that you could refute it today.” Andrei blushed in the dark. “A little,” he admitted. “And?” he asked. “What's the result if you weigh up the arguments?”
In conclusion, it can be said that your last argument outweighs all the others. Yes. Of course yes. Yes, yes, yes.

When they came back into the garden, hand in hand, with the gold bee ring on Lena's finger, the music stopped. A hundred people turned round. Mara, with the crown from the church still in her hair, was the first to see the ring and screamed so loudly that the neighbours in the house opposite switched on their lights. Dan stood up, came over to his son and hugged him, without a word, with his big hands that smelled of honey. Elena cried for the third time that day. And in Berlin, in the café “Bei Ingrid”, where the laptop was still on because Andrei had forgotten to end the call, Ludwig and Grete saw everything, on a small, shaky picture. Ludwig took the old brass bell out of his pocket. And he rang it, once, loud and clear, in an empty café in Prenzlauer Berg, at midnight, for a granddaughter in Transylvania who had just said yes.

Write an Erörterung (180–220 words) on one of these topics: “Sollte das Studium kostenlos sein?”, “Ist Homeoffice die Zukunft?” or “Sollten Großstädte autofrei werden?”. Follow the structure: introduction, 2 arguments for, 1–2 against with a refutation, conclusion.
I started with an introduction that shows why the topic is relevant now.
I used at least 3 formulas for arguments (Für … spricht, Darüber hinaus, Nicht zuletzt).
I presented an objection (Kritiker wenden ein…) and answered it (Dem ist entgegenzuhalten…).
I gave evidence or an example (Studien belegen… / Dies zeigt sich daran…).
I ended without new arguments (Abschließend lässt sich festhalten…).
In many big cities there is a debate about whether cars should be banned from the centre.
The main argument for car-free centres is that the air becomes cleaner.
In addition, studies show that pedestrian zones bring life to local shops.

In conclusion, it can be said that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided alternatives are created.
